newsitem.title: USA: Mail Boxes settles suits, to take charge.
newsitem.headline: Mail Boxes settles suits, to take charge.

text.p: Mail Boxes Etc said Friday it reached an overall settlement agreement in franchisee lawsuits involving the owners of 33 former Mail Boxes Etc centers and one current center, adding it will be reflected in a charge.
Under the agreement, Mail Boxes said, it will pay $4 million in cash and deliver about 41,000 restricted common shares.
The settlement will be reflected in the company's results for the second quarter, ended October 31. The financial results are expected to be released next week.
The charge for the settlement will be nearly $5 million pretax, "less than $3" million after tax, Chief Financial Officer Gary S. Grahn told Reuters.
Except for the charge, Mail Boxes Etc said, "second- quarter operating results are expected to be in line with the company's expectations."
Asked what those expectations were, Grahn said the company was referring to street estimates calling for growth of 20 percent plus, adding "we have generally agreed with that."
In last year's second quarter, the company earned $2.1 million, or $0.18 per share.
The First Call concensus estimate for the latest quarter is $0.22 per share.
The company said the agreement will settle all of the claims of the 34 franchise owners in the lawsuits, which have been in various phases of litigation.

The agreement resolves all the complaints without any admission of liability on the part of the company, Mail Boxes Etc said. It was also agreed that all franchisees involved in the lawsuit who are no longer in the Mail Boxes Etc franchise system would completely remove any remaining Mail Boxes Etc trademarks and logos from their stores.
The company noted that after three years of litigation efforts, trial had commenced on only four of the 34 franchises involved in the lawsuits.

In view of the legal fees that would be incurred by the company in litigating the remaining 30 cases, the distraction of management by the lawsuits and the inherent uncertainties in the outcome of any litigation, the executive committee of the board decided that an overall settlement was in the best interests of the company's shareholders, it said.
The legal fees have totaled "roughly $2 million" the past 18 months, a company spokesman said.
